Romanian Business News - ACTMedia :: Services | About us | Contact | RSS Home Daily Financial & banking Economic Companies Energy & Environment Drone explodes 100 metres inside Bulgaria after crossing from Romania Bulgaria's Prime Minister Rumen Radev said at a briefing following a meeting of the Security Council under the Council of Ministers that at 08:10hrs on Saturday morning, a drone entered Bulgarian airspace from the north, and exploded approximately 100 metres inside Bulgarian territory, acording to the BTA Bulgarian National News Agency. The incident occurred in the immediate vicinity of the former Kardam border checkpoint between Bulgaria and Romania, and about 1,000 metres from Bulgaria's compressor station on the Trans-Balkan gas pipeline route, Radev added. According to the prime minister, the drone crashed in a sunflower field. The area has been cordoned off. There were no casualties reported and no damage to infrastructure, Radev said. "Sound from the drone was detected by Romania's Border Police, followed by a loud explosion heard by the [Bulgarian] border patrol from General Toshevo, which is stationed in the area," said Radev. The location of the drone explosion was immediately identified, and teams from the Border Police, National Police and the Defence Ministry are currently at the site to determine the type of drone involved. He stressed that the drone in question had not been detected in Romanian or Bulgarian airspace. "We have also received no information from the Combined Air Operations Centre in Torrejon [Spain], which monitors the airspace across southern Europe," Radev added. Following the incident, he said, Border Police personnel and equipment used to detect and counter drones would be redeployed from the Turkish border to the Romanian border. Radev also commented on the three Shahed drones shot down in Romania two weeks ago, assuring reporters that Bulgaria had responded immediately and that the Defence Ministry had strengthened radar coverage in the region. Early next week, a meeting of the North Atlantic Council will be held, where Poland will provide information on the incident involving ballistic missiles on its territory, Romania will brief allies on the drones detected over its territory, and Bulgaria will raise the issue of the drone that exploded on Bulgarian territory, Radev said. Asked whether the drone was civilian or military, Radev said there was photographic material available, but because the drone had been damaged in the explosion, it was not possible to determine its type. "This is not a toy drone, it is a larger drone," he explained. Asked whether the incident was a deliberate attack and whether the drone had been carrying anything, he replied that this could not be established at this stage. He added that the drone had been carrying a substantial amount of explosive material, enough to produce an explosion that could be heard from a considerable distance. Radev explained that the drone had not been detected in either Bulgarian or Romanian airspace because such drones are difficult to detect due to their small size. "When flying at low altitude," he said, "it is not possible to ensure sufficiently dense radar coverage." There is currently information about only one drone. Radev also said that the procedure for procuring modern digital three-dimensional radars has been delayed, but the Defence Ministry is doing everything possible to speed up their delivery. Romania's Ministry of National Defense (MApN) says, in relation to the explosion that occurred in Bulgaria on Saturday, around 08:20hrs in the vicinity of the border with Romania, that its radar surveillance systems did not detect any aerial vehicle that crossed the Romanian airspace to Bulgaria. "In connection with the explosion that occurred on the territory of Bulgaria, on August 8, around 08:20, in the vicinity of the border with Romania, the Ministry of National Defense specifies that the radar surveillance systems of the MApN did not detect any aerial vehicle that crossed the airspace of Romania to Bulgaria. Also, in the time interval prior to the explosion, there were no developments of air targets indicating a possible trajectory through the national airspace towards the territory of Bulgaria," reads a MApN press release issued on Saturday. The ministry added that "it permanently monitors the situation in the vicinity of Romania's borders and will communicate, to the extent that relevant information will appear, additional data." https://www.politico.eu/article/state-of.text: BRUSSELS — Walk through the EU Quarter of Brussels and you’ll see posters plastered on walls and telephone poles asking European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen to give animal welfare a starring role in her State of the European Union address. “Your words matter,” the posters read. “Include animals in your speech.” As von der Leyen prepares for her big speech on Sept. 16, everyone from the largest lobby groups to cash-strapped NGOs — and even apparently guerrilla campaigners (none of the big animal welfare groups POLITICO spoke to took responsibility for the posters) — are making their pitch for a few precious seconds of the Commission president’s time. Advertisement Advertisement Some are taking the conventional approach. Last month, almost 200 industry associations and national groups signed a letter addressed to von der Leyen demanding she use her speech to commission an expansive, Mario Draghi-style report into the bloc’s appetite for fossil fuels. Others are a little more in-your-face. Alcohol lobby group SpiritsEurope has set up shop at Place du Luxembourg, where it has organized four days’ worth of events and — naturally — drinks receptions. It also conducted a competitiveness “temperature check” among its members to see how they are feeling, and to hammer home the point that the Commission could be listening more to the demands of an industry that feels somewhat overlooked. Von der Leyen “can bend the system to her will,” said SpiritsEurope Director General Mark Titterington. “That’s why we take the speech so seriously.” “It sets the direction, sets the tempo and helps to condition the environment,” he added. “The words that are in there are pored over for meaning.” Yet it’s not just the words in the speech that lobbyists and advocates are interested in — it’s the broader message. “We’re not looking for the president simply to say the word ‘health’,” said Milka Sokolović, director general at EPHA, an EU-wide public health NGO. Advertisement Advertisement She added that despite cuts to the organization — the health NGO has lost 40% of its staff since the Commission slashed its grants last year — it has been making “very concrete asks directly to the Commission, including von der Leyen, on the substance we would expect the speech to reflect.” That’s in part because the speech acts as a litmus test of what messages have actually cut through. “When specific asks have already been made through the normal channels, the SOTEU is an opportunity for the president to show whether they have translated into political priorities,” Sokolović said. Von der Leyen “keeps her cards exceedingly close to her chest in the whole process,” said one former European Commission cabinet member. | Martin Bertrand/Hans Lucas/AFP via Getty Images “A mention in that speech is not symbolic; it sends a signal to commissioners, to member states and to the Council that this file matters to the institution’s leadership,” said Animal Equality’s Vice-President of Europe Matteo Cupi. Failure to get a mention in the State of the European Union doesn’t mean a topic isn’t important — but a line in the speech does show political will to take action. “Legislation, budgets and implementation create the actual change,” said Sokolović. “But high-level political commitments set the direction. They decide what gets political attention and momentum in the first place. That is why the SOTEU matters.” Advertisement Advertisement “A mention is a signal, a specific commitment is politically meaningful, a commitment with a deliverable and timetable is the real outcome.” But whether lobbyists can even get the access that matters is another question. The Commission president “keeps her cards exceedingly close to her chest in the whole process,” said one former Commission cabinet member, granted anonymity to speak freely. “In the end, von der Leyen writes the whole thing herself — there are literally four people involved,” the person said, adding that the speech is written only in the few days before it’s presented. Among the few who do enjoy open access to the Commission’s upper echelons — such as chemicals lobby Cefic — the SOTEU is an “important milestone,” but still only “one step in a broader policy cycle,” said a spokesperson for the group. “What ultimately matters is how political priorities are translated into concrete measures and implemented in practice.” Tech CEOs have also kept a direct line into von der Leyen. Their main lobby group, DigitalEurope, counted a mention of its AI & Tech Declaration in last year’s speech as an “important signal that industry’s voice was being heard,” said Director General Cecilia Bonefeld-Dahl. She also said the presence of Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney at this year’s event is “a real opportunity to take the EU-Canada partnership to the next level,” with the lobby group keen to act as “a bridge” between Europe and its international partners. Advertisement Advertisement One reason why the speech is so important for lobbyists and NGOs is that there are sometimes surprises within. In 2023’s edition, for example, von der Leyen dropped a bombshell , announcing an anti-subsidy probe into Chinese electric vehicles. European carmakers’ stocks spiked within the hour. Pauline Bastidon, SpiritsEurope’s director of competitiveness and trade, said one upshot of that announcement was a retaliatory move by China into the EU alcohol sector. “We are still paying the price for that,” she said. “There can be some very concrete consequences for what is said in the SOTEU speech.” Additional reporting by Gerardo Fortuna and Max Griera .

https://www.theguardian.com/uk-news/2026.text: Court sketch of Royal Navy sailor Teddy Young appearing at Westminster magistrates' court in London Photograph: Elizabeth Cook/PA View image in fullscreen Court sketch of Royal Navy sailor Teddy Young appearing at Westminster magistrates' court in London Photograph: Elizabeth Cook/PA UK news Royal Navy member appears in court charged with spying for Russia Teddy Young, 24, from Bedfordshire, accused of drafting a message in Russian containing classified information Ben Quinn Thu 8 Oct 2026 07.53 EDT First published on Thu 8 Oct 2026 03.14 EDT Share Prefer the Guardian on Google A serving member of the Royal Navy has appeared in court charged with spying for Russia. Teddy Young, 24, was accused of obtaining protected information that could benefit an unnamed foreign power. He was arrested at his home in Bedfordshire on Tuesday after an investigation by Counter Terrorism Policing London (CTPL). He had been charged with offences under the National Security Act, the Metropolitan police said on Thursday. Young, a naval intelligence rating, is alleged to have abused high-level security clearance to access secret defence and intelligence data after being deployed on a navy vessel. He is accused of drafting a message in Russian containing classified information and had allegedly taken steps to make direct contact with the Russian authorities. Young was first arrested in May last year. At that point he was suspended and relieved of his duties, and he was on gardening leave until his latest arrest. Young appeared at Westminster magistrates court wearing a grey navy tracksuit, and he spoke only to confirm his name. While there was no application for bail, the district judge Annabelle Pilling told Young: “On the basis of the information I have already read, there are substantial grounds to believe that if granted bail you would not come back to court and that you would make efforts to avoid further court appearances and would commit further offences.” Young was remanded in custody to appear before a specialist judge at the Old Bailey on 16 October. The Crown Prosecution Service authorised the charges on Wednesday. They allege that between 26 November 2024 and 21 May 2025 Young engaged in conduct in preparation for committing an offence of disclosing protected information. It is also alleged that in the same period he obtained, copied, recorded or retained protected information, intending the conduct to benefit a foreign power. Commander Helen Flanagan, the head of CTPL, said in a statement issued before the court appearance: “These are very serious charges against a serving member of the armed forces. We have worked extremely closely with relevant operational colleagues within the Ministry of Defence as our investigation has progressed to ensure appropriate measures could be taken to mitigate any potential risks linked to this matter.” The arrest and charges are not connected to the recent investigation into an incident at RAF Fairford. A Royal Navy spokesperson said: “A member of the Royal Navy has been charged with National Security Act offences following an investigation by Counter Terrorism Policing London. As legal proceedings are ongoing, it would be inappropriate to comment further at this stage.” Explore more on these topics UK news news Share Reuse this content Most viewed Most viewed UK UK politics Education Media Society Law Scotland Wales Northern Ireland

https://balkaninsight.com/2026/10/12/eus.text: According to Liberties’ analysis, at least 96 per cent of the EU Commission’s recommendations have not been fully implemented, and 54 per cent show no or only limited progress. Henna Virkkunen, Executive Vice-President of the European Commission, and Michael McGrath, European Commissioner, hold press conference on the Rule of Law report, on 17 July 2026. Photo: EC The European Commission’s annual Rule of Law Report aims to identify emerging threats and prompt governments to address them before they escalate. But the failure to implement its recommendations raises questions about its ability to bring about meaningful change, according to the latest analysis by the Civil Liberties Union for Europe. Liberties’ 2026 Rule of Law Gap Analysis , published on Monday, examines where the European Commission’s report falls short, assessing the implementation of country-specific recommendations while exploring its potential to prevent democratic decline and support the restoration of the rule of law. According to the NGO’s analysis, at least 96 per cent of the European Commission’s recommendations have not been fully implemented, and 54 per cent show no or only limited progress, meaning the implementation gap “remains persistent and significant”. The lack of implementation means that 96 per cent of the recommendations issued in 2026 were repeated from previous years, with 65 per cent dating back to 2022. “Now in its seventh year, the European Commission’s annual Rule of Law Report is an important assessment of the state of the rule of law across the Union,” notes Liberties. “This year’s Gap Analysis again points to a significant implementation gap and a failure to surface and address critical issues, whether at the national level or cross-cutting issues that impact the rule of law across the [European] Union.” Liberties also addresses what it calls the European Commission’s “overly optimistic assessment” in this year’s report, where it claimed that “nearly 1 in 2 (47%) of the recommendations made in 2025 have since been addressed by Member States – either fully or partially”. In reality, the NGO says, this disguises a wide range of partial implementation and fails to unpack why some problems remain so entrenched. Liberties criticises what it calls the EU’s “fragmented toolbox” for fighting democratic backsliding. The EU has various rule-of-law instruments at its disposal – infringement proceedings, Article 7, etc. – but what is missing is “an overarching framework that ties these instruments together”. “The Rule of Law Report has the potential to provide that comprehensive overview, but risks instead becoming a ‘leftover tool’ – one that only picks up issues if unaddressed by the EU’s other mechanisms. As things stand, it fails to offer a comprehensive picture of the problems at hand nor a clear pathway to recovery, as illustrated by [our] case study on Hungary,” it says. That case study looks at how Hungary’s political transition presents an opportunity to rethink how the Rule of Law Report can guide reforms and assess whether institutional safeguards work in practice. Liberties also cites the decision to remove recommendations related to the European Media Freedom Act (EMFA), because most of its provisions became legally binding for member states in August 2025, requiring all countries to effectively implement its provisions. “Consequently, the share of recommendations on ‘Media freedom and pluralism’ declined significantly, now accounting for only 6% of all recommendations, compared with 16-22% in previous years,” it notes. “However, it is unclear at this stage,” it says, “whether removing these recommendations best serves the defence of media freedom and pluralism.” For example, Liberties’ partners in Bulgaria, Croatia and Spain report continued political interference in the public service media, while they highlight in Croatia, Italy, Malta and Romania continued opaque media ownership structures, often with no legislative steps planned to address the issues. “In Slovakia, actions by the government appear to be deepening existing EMFA violations rather than constructively addressing them,” it says. Photo: Star/file Bangladesh’s garment exports to Poland are rising as the Russia-Ukraine war disrupts direct trade with Russia and buyers shift sourcing from China, even as shipments to several major markets face pressure. Garment exports to Poland grew 9.8 percent year-on-year to $1.86 billion in fiscal year 2025-26 (FY26), according to Export Promotion Bureau (EPB) data. Tap here to add The Daily Star as a trusted source In contrast, Bangladesh’s total garment exports fell 1.64 percent during the fiscal year. The slowdown has continued in major destinations. Bangladesh’s garment exports to the US fell 5.3 percent in the first half of 2026, while shipments to the European Union declined 11.67 percent in the first eight months, according to World Bank and Eurostat data. Industry leaders attribute the growth in exports to Poland partly to Polish buyers re-exporting garments to neighbouring Russia, where sanctions-related payment difficulties have complicated direct trade. They also cite demand for basic garment items and opportunities created by Chinese suppliers losing orders. A GROWING MARKET Bangladesh exported garment items worth $1.38 billion to Poland in FY21, with the amount rising to $2 billion in FY22, according to EPB data. Exports fell to $1.40 billion in FY23 before recovering to $1.54 billion in FY24 and $1.69 billion in FY25. In contrast, garment exports to Russia have declined since the war began in February 2022. Before the war, Bangladesh exported more than $665 million worth of garment items to Russia in FY21, with industry players considering it as a rising market for Bangladeshi apparels. Exports to the country have since continued to fall, standing at $257.26 million in FY26. POLAND AS A ROUTE TO RUSSIA Mahmud Hasan Khan, president of the Bangladesh Garment Manufacturers and Exporters Association (BGMEA), said a significant volume of garment items was being re-exported from Poland to Russia. Before the Russia-Ukraine war, Turkish traders also imported Bangladeshi garments for re-export to Russia, he said. Exports to Turkey declined after the country imposed a 17 percent duty on Bangladeshi garment items in 2011, according to him. After the war began, Polish importers started re-exporting garments to Russia, contributing to the growth in Bangladesh’s exports to Poland, said Mahmud. Salah Uddin Ahmed, managing director of IFS Texwear (Pvt) Ltd, which exports nearly $2 million worth of knitwear a month, also said some Polish buyers sourcing garments from Bangladesh also re-export products to Russia. He, however, said he did not have specific evidence confirming that the garments being re-exported to Russia were sourced from Bangladesh. Mohammad Hatem, president of the Bangladesh Knitwear Manufacturers and Exporters Association (BKMEA), said Poland could serve as a third country for exporting garments to Russia. Western sanctions imposed after Russia’s invasion of Ukraine restricted several Russian banks’ access to the SWIFT international financial messaging system. The restrictions complicated some cross-border payment arrangements, making it harder for Bangladeshi exporters to receive payments from Russian buyers. For all latest news, follow The Daily Star's Google News channel. The war has also disrupted payments involving buyers linked to Russia. 28 Bangladeshi garment exporters have been struggling to recover $5.2 million from a Polish buyer for nearly two years, said Mijanur Rahman, managing director of Fabrica Knit Composite Ltd and a vice-president of the BGMEA. Mijanur, who has been coordinating efforts to resolve the payment issue, said the buyer’s business had been disrupted by the war. CHINA’S LOST ORDERS, BASICWEAR DEMAND Exporters say the rise in shipments to Poland is not solely linked to the Russia-Ukraine war. According to Mijanur, the loss of work orders by Chinese suppliers was one of the reasons behind the increase in Bangladesh’s garment exports to Poland. Demand for basic garment items in the market was also strong, he added. IFS Texwear’s Salah Uddin, meanwhile, noted that Poland was a growing market for Bangladeshi exporters because they enjoy zero-duty access under the European Union’s trade arrangements. The duty advantage, combined with demand for basic garments and possible shifts in sourcing from China, has supported Bangladesh’s exports to Poland, exporters said.
